summary: Gives guidelines for using EPP's extension mechanisms to add new features and new object types. EPP is an XML protocol with a generic framework, so careful extension keeps it consistent. It is informational advice for those writing extensions.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3735 explains how to extend the Extensible Provisioning Protocol, the XML protocol registries and registrars use to manage domain names and similar objects. It says what an extension may and may not do, how each extension is named, how a server tells clients what it supports, and which of three kinds of extension to reach for first.

questions: when to create a new object mapping
when should a new epp extension be an object mapping
how does an epp server announce an extension
subtitle: How to add a new feature to the Extensible Provisioning Protocol without breaking it

tldr.problem: EPP was built to be extended, but XML offers several ways to extend a protocol and most of the wrong choices produce something that does not interoperate or that quietly becomes a new version of the protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets out what counts as an extension, how an extension is identified by a URI, how a server announces the extensions it offers and how a client asks to use one, and a sequence of three questions that lead a designer from the least disruptive extension form to the most.
tldr.outcome: It is guidance rather than a specification, written for designers choosing EPP for a provisioning problem, but usable by anyone representing an IETF protocol in XML.

today: RFC 3735 is an Informational memo published in March 2004, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is advice for extension designers, and the protocol it describes is RFC 3730.

sections.title: Why EPP Was Built to Be Extended
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol was originally designed to provide a standard Internet domain name registration protocol for use between domain name registrars and domain name registries. Several design decisions were made so that the protocol could also be used in other provisioning environments. Extensibility was a design goal from the very beginning: EPP is represented in XML and specified in XML Schema, with XML namespaces used to identify protocol grammars. The core protocol specification describes general protocol functions rather than objects to be managed, and managed object definitions, such as the mapping for Internet domain names, are loosely coupled to the core specification. A concentrated effort was made to separate required minimum protocol functionality from object management operating logic. Several extension mechanisms were included so that designers could add new features or customise existing ones for different operating environments.

The document describes those mechanisms in detail and gives guidelines for using them. It was written for protocol designers considering EPP as the solution to a provisioning problem, but anyone interested in using XML to represent IETF protocols may find the guidelines useful. XML is case sensitive, and unless stated otherwise the XML instances and examples in the document must be interpreted in the character case presented.
sections.plainLanguage: EPP was written for registering domain names, but on purpose it was built so that the same machinery could manage other kinds of object. That is why the rules about how to extend it are worth writing down carefully.

sections.title: What Counts as an Extension
sections.content:
The EPP extension model is based on the XML representation for a wildcard schema component using an any element information item, together with XML namespaces.

Extending a protocol implies adding features without changing the protocol itself. In EPP that means an extension MUST NOT alter an existing protocol schema, because such changes result in new versions of an existing schema rather than extensions of one. A designer MUST NOT add new elements to an existing schema and call the result an extension: the result is a new, not backwards-compatible, version of the existing schema. Extensions must adhere to the principles of this section to be valid protocol extensions.

EPP extensions must be specified in XML, which ensures that parsers capable of processing EPP structures are also capable of processing EPP extensions. A designer must also remember that extensions themselves may be extensible, and that a good chain of extensions is one in which the protocol schemas evolve from general functionality to more specific, perhaps even more limited, functionality.

On documentation, the EPP core specification has an appendix with a suggested outline for extension documents. Designers are free to use that template or any other format, but the extension document should at least address all the topics in the template. Designers need to consider the intended audience and consumers of their extensions. Extensions may be documented as Internet-Drafts and RFCs when there is a need for coordination, interoperability and broad distribution, and the intended maturity level depends on what is being extended and on the amount of general interest. Extensions need not be published as Internet-Drafts or RFCs if they are intended for operation in a closed environment or for a limited audience, and in that case they may be documented in a file and structural format appropriate for the audience.
sections.plainLanguage: The line the document draws is between adding to a protocol and changing it. If you change the schema of what already exists, you have made a new version, not an extension. An extension is a separate piece, written in XML, with its own name.

sections.title: Identifying an Extension
sections.content:
An EPP extension is uniquely identified by a Uniform Resource Identifier. The URI used to identify the extension must also be used to identify the XML namespace associated with the extension. Any valid URI may be used, though the choice of form, a URL or a URN, hierarchical or relative, should depend on factors such as the organisation's policies on change control and a balance between locating resources and the need for persistence. An extension namespace may describe several extension mechanisms, such as the definition of new protocol features, objects or elements, within the schema used to define the namespace.

The sample extension-identifying URIs given are urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:foo-ext1 and http://custom/obj1ext-1.0. Designers may include version information in the URI, and if they do, the URI itself will need to change as the extension is revised.

URIs for extensions intended for the IETF standards track must conform to the URN syntax specifications and registration procedures described in the IETF XML Registry. URIs for extensions that are not intended for the standards track must conform to the URI syntax specifications described in RFC 2396.
sections.plainLanguage: Every extension has a URI, and the same URI names the XML namespace it uses. The document explains which form of URI to pick, and the rule that an extension meant for the standards track must use a URN of the registered kind.

sections.title: Announcing and Selecting Extensions
sections.content:
An EPP server must announce the extensions available for client use as part of a greeting element, sent to a client before the client establishes an interactive session. The greeting element contains zero or more svcExtension elements which, if present, contain a URI identifying an available extension. In the example in the document, the server announces two extensions.

An EPP client must establish a session with an EPP server using the EPP login command before attempting to use any standard commands or extensions. The login command contains zero or more svcExtension elements which, if present, contain a URI identifying an available extension that the client wishes to use during the session. An EPP server must announce all extensions that are publicly available for client use, and a client must not request an extension that the server has not announced. A server may restrict a client's ability to select an extension based on the client's identity and the authorizations granted by the server operator.

Three levels of extension exist. A protocol-level extension adds structures to the protocol itself, by defining a schema for the new structures and assigning a URI to identify the object namespace and schema. An object-level extension defines a new kind of object to manage, with its own schema and URI, and it is the form used when the existing command and response structures can be reused for a new object. A command-response extension adds elements to command and response structures that already exist, for example extending the domain name mapping to cover domain names that represent E.164 telephone numbers. Some object mappings, such as the domain name mapping, include elements that associate authentication information with an object, and the schema for a mapping that supports it should be flexible enough to specify multiple forms of authentication information, which with XML Schema can be done by offering an element choice that includes an any element information item.
sections.plainLanguage: A server lists the extensions it offers in its greeting, and a client asks for the ones it wants to use when it logs in. A client must not ask for something the server never offered. Extensions come at three levels: adding to the protocol, defining a new kind of object, or adding to the commands of an object that already exists.

sections.title: Choosing an Extension Mechanism
sections.content:
Extensibility is a powerful feature of XML, and it also provides multiple opportunities to make poor design decisions. There are typically several ways to accomplish a single task, and while all of them may work for some definition of working, one extension form will usually be more appropriate than the others. The document gives a sequence of steps.

The first form to explore is the command-response extension, because adding elements to an existing object mapping is the simplest form available. The first question is whether the task can be accomplished by adding to an existing object mapping or changing an existing object mapping slightly. If yes, extend the existing mapping. Knowing where to find object mappings is critical to answering this, and the document lists the archives: the IETF, where mappings and extensions have been documented in RFCs and Internet-Drafts; IANA, with the IETF XML Registry; OASIS; XML.org; and other archives that are likely in the future.

If there is no existing object mapping that can be extended, consider an object-level extension and ask whether the task can be accomplished using the existing EPP command and response structures applied to a new object. A new object mapping should differ significantly from existing ones, and if it replicates a significant number of structures found in an existing mapping the command-response question was probably answered incorrectly.

If neither works, consider a protocol-level extension and ask whether the task can be accomplished by adding new EPP commands, responses or other structures applied to new or existing objects. If the answer is no, EPP cannot be used directly for the task. The forms are listed in order of complexity, and selecting one without careful consideration can add complexity without any gain in functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives three questions in order, from the smallest change to the largest: can I add to a mapping that already exists, can I use the existing commands for a new kind of object, or do I need new commands in the protocol itself. The advice is to try the smallest change first.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
EPP extensions inherit the security services of the protocol structure being extended. An extension of an object mapping inherits all of the security services of that object mapping. Extensions may specify additional security services, such as services for peer entity authentication, confidentiality, data integrity, authorization, access control or non-repudiation, but they must not mandate the removal of security services available in the protocol structure being extended. Protocol designers developing extensions need to be aware of the security threats in their intended operating environment so that appropriate services can be provided, and guidelines for writing a Security Considerations section are in RFC 3552.

EPP is represented in XML, which requires conforming parsers to recognise both UTF-8 and UTF-16, with support for other character encodings also possible. EPP extensions must observe both the internationalization considerations in the EPP core protocol specification and IETF policy on the use of character sets and languages.
sections.plainLanguage: An extension cannot quietly drop the protections the protocol already has, though it may add more, such as confidentiality or integrity checks. Extensions also have to follow the same rules about character sets as the rest of EPP.
